- `format.preview` — Enables upcoming formatting styles. [Docs](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/formatter/#preview-style)
- `nested-string-quote-style` — With `"preferred"` on Python 3.12+, uses the configured quote style for nested strings. [Docs](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/formatter/#quotes)
- `extension` — Maps additional file extensions to Markdown for code-block formatting. [Docs](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/formatter/#markdown-code-formatting)
- `extend-exclude` — Excludes files from formatting, such as `*.md`. [Docs](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/formatter/#markdown-code-formatting)
- `--check` — Checks formatting without writing files; exits nonzero when changes are needed. [Docs](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/formatter/#ruff-format)
- `--exit-non-zero-on-format` — Returns exit code 1 when files were formatted. [Docs](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/formatter/#exit-codes)

Here are all **19 pages** in the current Pydantic Concepts section, in navigation order:

1. **[Models](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/models/)** — Define structured data using `BaseModel` classes and type annotations. Covers validation, nested and generic models, copying, extra fields, immutability, and dynamically creating models.

2. **[Fields](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/fields/)** — Customize individual fields with `Field()` and `Annotated`: defaults, constraints, aliases, and schema metadata. Also explains computed fields, deprecated fields, and controlling field visibility or mutation.

3. **[JSON Schema](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/json_schema/)** — Generate JSON Schema from models or other supported types. Shows how to customize descriptions, titles, references, and schema generation for validation versus serialization.

4. **[JSON](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/json/)** — Parse and validate JSON directly using Pydantic’s built-in parser, and serialize data back to JSON. Covers partial JSON parsing and string caching for performance.

5. **[Types](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/types/)** — Explains how types determine validation and serialization behavior. Covers reusable constrained types, named aliases, utility annotations, and custom types with advanced schema hooks.

6. **[Unions](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/unions/)** — Explains how Pydantic chooses between possible types: left-to-right matching, smart matching, or discriminators. Discriminated unions select a specific variant using a tag or callable, making validation more predictable.

7. **[Alias](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/alias/)** — Map Python field names to different names in incoming or outgoing data. Covers nested input paths, alternative input names, automatic alias generators, and precedence rules.

8. **[Configuration](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/config/)** — Control Pydantic behavior through configuration on models, dataclasses, type adapters, and validated functions. Explains inheritance and how configuration propagates across type boundaries.

9. **[Serialization](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/serialization/)** — Export data as Python objects or JSON, with control over which fields appear. Covers custom field and model serializers, serialization context, and handling subclasses.

10. **[Validators](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/validators/)** — Add custom checks and transformations at the field or model level. Explains validator modes, execution order, access to other validated data, context, and raising validation errors.

11. **[Dataclasses](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/dataclasses/)** — Add Pydantic validation to dataclasses using its `@dataclass` decorator. Covers configuration, standard-library dataclass integration, initialization hooks, and differences from models.

12. **[Forward Annotations](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/forward_annotations/)** — Reference types that are defined later, including recursive models. Explains Python-version differences in annotation evaluation and handling cyclic references or imports.

13. **[Strict Mode](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/strict_mode/)** — Reduce automatic type conversion so incorrect input types produce errors. Enable it per validation call, field, or model; some JSON representations remain accepted even in strict mode.

14. **[Type Adapter](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/type_adapter/)** — Validate, serialize, and generate JSON Schema for types without creating a `BaseModel`. Useful for primitives, dataclasses, `TypedDict`s, and collections such as `list[User]`.

15. **[Validation Decorator](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/validation_decorator/)** — Use `@validate_call` to validate function arguments from their annotations, with optional return-value validation. Covers supported signatures, async functions, configuration, and performance limitations.

16. **[Conversion Table](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/conversion_table/)** — A reference for accepted input types and conversions for each target type. Distinguishes Python from JSON input and shows which conversions strict mode permits.

17. **[Settings Management](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/pydantic_settings/)** — Use the separate `pydantic-settings` package to load validated application configuration. Covers environment variables, `.env` files, secrets, configuration files, CLI arguments, and source priority.

18. **[Performance](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/performance/)** — Practical ways to reduce validation overhead when profiling shows it matters. Includes direct JSON validation, reusing type adapters, choosing simpler structures, tagged unions, and failing early.

19. **[Experimental](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/experimental/)** — Introduces features still subject to change or removal, including validation pipelines, partial validation, and callable-argument validation. Explains their usage and current limitations.

answer:
**Intermittent fasting doesn’t inevitably cause muscle loss.** Studies combining fasting with resistance training generally find preserved lean mass and strength. But some trials without those supports report lean-mass loss. These three papers show the range:

1. **Ho et al. (2024), *Nutrients* — systematic review and meta-analysis.** Seven studies, 164 participants: time-restricted eating plus resistance training reduced fat mass, with **no statistically significant difference in muscle mass or strength** versus conventional eating plus training. Reassuring, though the evidence base was small. [Read the paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11434652/)

2. **Keenan et al. (2022), *European Journal of Nutrition* — 12-week trial.** Thirty-four participants completed resistance training with either 5:2 fasting or daily calorie restriction; both groups were prescribed at least 1.4 g protein/kg/day on average. **Both gained lean mass and strength**, without significant differences in those outcomes. One thigh-muscle-area measure favored daily restriction. [Read the paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9106626/)

3. **Lowe et al. (2020), *JAMA Internal Medicine* — TREAT randomized trial.** Compared noon–8 p.m. eating with three structured meals daily for 12 weeks. In the 50-person body-composition subgroup, fasting produced **greater loss of arm-and-leg lean mass**. Total lean-mass loss did **not** differ significantly between groups. Protein intake wasn’t measured, limiting explanations for the finding. [Read the paper](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/2771095)

My reading: resistance training and adequate protein are central considerations when fasting during weight loss. The evidence is more reassuring for preserving muscle than for maximizing muscle growth. Also, **lean mass is a proxy for muscle**, including water and other tissues; these findings shouldn’t be extrapolated to prolonged, multiday fasts.

The current Pydantic docs have **19 Concepts pages**, listed here in navigation order.

1. **[Models](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/models/)** — Define structured data using `BaseModel` subclasses and annotated fields. Covers validation, nested and generic models, copying, inheritance, and dynamically creating models.

2. **[Fields](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/fields/)** — Customize individual fields with defaults, constraints, aliases, and metadata using `Field()` and `Annotated`. Also covers computed fields, immutability, deprecation, and excluding fields from output.

3. **[JSON Schema](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/json_schema/)** — Generate JSON Schema from models or other supported types to describe their expected structure. Explains customization through field metadata, annotations, hooks, and schema generators.

4. **[JSON](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/json/)** — Parse and validate JSON directly with Pydantic’s built-in parser, and serialize data back to JSON. Includes partial JSON parsing, strict-mode behavior, and string caching.

5. **[Types](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/types/)** — Explains how types control validation and serialization, from standard Python types to Pydantic’s specialized types. Shows how to build reusable custom types with `Annotated`, named aliases, and schema hooks.

6. **[Unions](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/unions/)** — Explains how Pydantic chooses among multiple permitted types using left-to-right, smart, or discriminated union validation. Covers discriminator fields and callables, nested unions, and validation errors.

7. **[Alias](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/alias/)** — Map external field names to Python attributes, with separate aliases for validation and serialization. Covers nested input paths, alternative names, automatic alias generation, and precedence rules.

8. **[Configuration](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/config/)** — Control Pydantic behavior through settings such as `ConfigDict` on models, dataclasses, type adapters, and validated functions. Explains inheritance and how configuration propagates across type boundaries.

9. **[Serialization](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/serialization/)** — Convert validated objects into Python structures or JSON, choosing which fields to include. Covers custom field and model serializers, serialization context, and handling subclasses.

10. **[Validators](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/validators/)** — Add custom checks and transformations at the field or whole-model level. Explains before, after, plain, and wrap validators, their execution order, error reporting, and access to validation context.

11. **[Dataclasses](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/dataclasses/)** — Add Pydantic validation to dataclasses without using `BaseModel`. Covers configuration, standard-library dataclass interoperability, initialization hooks, and using `TypeAdapter` for serialization or schema generation.

12. **[Forward Annotations](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/forward_annotations/)** — Reference types before they are defined and build self-referencing or recursive models. Explains annotation behavior across Python versions, cyclic references, and cyclic imports.

13. **[Strict Mode](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/strict_mode/)** — Restrict automatic conversions so incorrect input types produce errors. Enable it per validation call, per field, or through configuration; some JSON representations remain accepted.

14. **[Type Adapter](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/type_adapter/)** — Validate, serialize, and generate schemas for types without creating a `BaseModel`. Useful for primitives, dataclasses, typed dictionaries, and collections such as `list[User]`.

15. **[Validation Decorator](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/validation_decorator/)** — Use `@validate_call` to validate and convert function arguments from their annotations before execution. Covers function signatures, async functions, configuration, and practical limitations.

16. **[Conversion Table](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/conversion_table/)** — A reference showing which input types each field type accepts and under what conditions. Distinguishes Python from JSON input and strict from lax validation.

17. **[Settings Management](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/pydantic_settings/)** — Use the separate `pydantic-settings` package to load validated application configuration from environment variables, dotenv files, secrets, and other sources. Covers source priority, nested settings, CLI support, and cloud secret stores.

18. **[Performance](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/performance/)** — Practical ways to reduce validation overhead when profiling shows it matters. Recommendations include direct JSON validation, reusing type adapters, concrete container types, tagged unions, and avoiding expensive validator patterns.

19. **[Experimental](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/experimental/)** — Introduces features that may change or disappear, including composable validation pipelines, partial validation, and callable-argument validation. Describes their usage and current limitations.

**Intermittent fasting can cause some lean-mass loss, but muscle loss isn’t inevitable.** Results depend on the fasting regimen, protein intake and resistance training. Also, “lean mass” includes water and other tissues—it isn’t a direct measurement of muscle alone.

These three papers give a useful balance:

1. **[“Efficiency of time-restricted eating and energy restriction…” (2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12487415/)** — A systematic review of 20 randomized trials involving 1,242 adults. Across the 16 trials reporting fat-free mass, time-restricted eating produced about **0.57 kg more fat-free-mass loss** than comparison diets. Crucially, the review excluded exercise interventions, so it doesn’t establish what happens when fasting is combined with lifting.

2. **[Lowe et al., “The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial” (2020)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7522780/)** — Compared eating from noon–8 p.m. with three structured meals daily for 12 weeks. In the small subgroup receiving body-composition scans, the fasting group lost **0.47 kg more arm-and-leg lean mass** than controls. Protein intake wasn’t measured, and exercise wasn’t prescribed, limiting explanations for the difference.

3. **[Keenan et al., “Intermittent fasting and continuous energy restriction result in similar changes…” (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9106626/)** — Compared 5:2 fasting with daily calorie restriction during 12 weeks of resistance training, with protein prescribed at approximately **1.4 g/kg/day**. Both groups improved lean mass and strength, with broadly similar outcomes. This supports the possibility of preserving—and gaining—muscle while fasting under those conditions.

My reading: **fasting alone doesn’t guarantee muscle preservation; results are more reassuring when resistance training and sufficient protein are built into the program.** These findings concern daily eating windows and 5:2 diets, and shouldn’t be generalized to prolonged multiday fasts.

Here are all **19 pages** in the current Pydantic **Concepts** section, in navigation order:

1. **[Models](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/models/)** — Define structured data using `BaseModel` subclasses and typed fields. Covers validation, nested and generic models, extra fields, copying, dynamic models, and custom root types.

2. **[Fields](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/fields/)** — Customize individual fields with defaults, constraints, aliases, and metadata using `Field()` and `Annotated`. Also explains strictness, immutability, deprecated fields, and computed fields.

3. **[JSON Schema](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/json_schema/)** — Generate JSON Schema from models or other supported types for documentation and tooling. Customize schema metadata, references, titles, and the generation process itself.

4. **[JSON](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/json/)** — Parse and validate JSON directly with Pydantic’s built-in parser, and serialize data back to JSON. Explains JSON-specific strictness behavior, partial parsing, and string caching.

5. **[Types](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/types/)** — Explains how Python types, Pydantic types, and utility annotations control validation and serialization. Shows how to build reusable constrained types and integrate custom types.

6. **[Unions](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/unions/)** — Explains how Pydantic chooses between alternative types: left-to-right matching, default “smart” matching, or discriminators. Covers tagged variants, nested unions, and interpreting validation errors.

7. **[Alias](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/alias/)** — Map external data names to Python field names, with separate aliases for input and output. Covers nested input paths, alternative names, automatic alias generation, and precedence rules.

8. **[Configuration](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/config/)** — Control Pydantic behavior through configuration on models, dataclasses, type adapters, and validated functions. Explains inheritance, shared defaults, and how configuration propagates across types.

9. **[Serialization](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/serialization/)** — Export models and other supported values as Python objects or JSON. Covers custom serializers, serialization context, subclass behavior, and selectively including or excluding fields.

10. **[Validators](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/validators/)** — Add custom checks and transformations to individual fields or whole models. Explains validator modes, execution order, error reporting, and access to other validated values or context.

11. **[Dataclasses](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/dataclasses/)** — Add Pydantic validation to dataclasses while retaining their familiar structure. Covers configuration, inheritance, initialization hooks, and using `TypeAdapter` for serialization and schema generation.

12. **[Forward Annotations](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/forward_annotations/)** — Reference types before they are defined and build self-referencing models. Explains annotation handling across Python versions, recursive structures, and cyclic imports.

13. **[Strict Mode](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/strict_mode/)** — Reject mismatched input types instead of applying the usual coercions. Enable strictness per validation call, field, or model; some JSON representations still receive special treatment.

14. **[Type Adapter](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/type_adapter/)** — Validate, serialize, and generate schemas for arbitrary types without defining a `BaseModel`. Useful for collections, dataclasses, `TypedDict`s, and standalone type annotations.

15. **[Validation Decorator](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/validation_decorator/)** — Use `@validate_call` to validate and coerce function arguments from their annotations. Covers different signatures, async functions, configuration, and performance limitations.

16. **[Conversion Table](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/conversion_table/)** — A reference showing which input types each field type accepts and under what conditions. Distinguishes Python from JSON input and lists conversions permitted in strict mode.

17. **[Settings Management](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/pydantic_settings/)** — Use the separate `pydantic-settings` package to load validated configuration from environment variables, dotenv files, secrets, and other sources. Covers source priority, nested settings, CLI support, and cloud secret stores.

18. **[Performance](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/performance/)** — Practical ways to reduce validation overhead, including direct JSON validation and reusing type adapters. Also discusses concrete container types, tagged unions, simpler structures, and avoiding expensive validators.

19. **[Experimental](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/experimental/)** — Introduces features still being evaluated, including composable validation pipelines, partial validation, and callable argument validation. Explains their usage and limitations; these APIs may change or be removed.

**Intermittent fasting doesn’t inevitably cause muscle loss.** These studies suggest muscle can be maintained when fasting is combined with resistance training and sufficient protein, but fasting alone has produced some concerning results. Three useful papers:

1. **[Ho et al., 2024 — Systematic review and meta-analysis of time-restricted feeding plus resistance training](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11434652/)**  
   Across **7 studies involving 164 adults**, restricting eating hours produced greater fat loss without a statistically significant difference in muscle mass or strength versus conventional eating plus lifting. Encouraging, but the studies were small and mostly lasted only 4–8 weeks.

2. **[Keenan et al., 2022 — Intermittent fasting versus continuous calorie restriction with resistance training](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9106626/)**  
   A **12-week randomized trial** compared 5:2 fasting with daily calorie restriction. Both groups trained and received diets targeting about **1.4 g protein/kg/day**. Both gained lean mass and strength, with broadly similar results. This shows fasting can coexist with muscle gain in previously untrained adults.

3. **[Lowe et al., 2020 — The TREAT randomized clinical trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7522780/)**  
   Compared noon-to-8-p.m. eating with three structured meals over **12 weeks**, without prescribing protein intake or resistance training. In the body-composition subgroup, fasting participants lost more arm-and-leg lean mass—about **0.47 kg more than controls**. The difference in total lean-mass loss between groups was not statistically significant.

My interpretation: **protein intake and resistance training deserve more attention than the eating window alone.** Also, “lean mass” includes water and other tissues, so a measured decline isn’t equivalent to the same amount of muscle loss. These results don’t establish what happens with prolonged, multiday fasting.
